response:
Transformer inference over long contexts requires storing past key-value pairs in a cache, but memory and compute constraints force systems to evict some of those entries — the central question is: which tokens' KV pairs can you safely discard without the model losing track of temporal relationships across the sequence? Learned retention scoring addresses this by training a predictor (often a lightweight head or auxiliary model) to estimate each token's future relevance, but this creates a subtle circularity: the scorer must predict importance before the downstream attention patterns that would reveal importance have occurred. The "temporal context compression artifact" is what happens when that scorer systematically fails at horizon boundaries — the model retains semantically salient tokens (nouns, named entities) but evicts positional glue (conjunctions, anaphora, temporal markers like "then" or "after that"), leaving the residual stream with a sequence that is lexically intact but temporally incoherent. A beginner sees compression as a retrieval problem — did we keep the right facts? — and misses that transformers encode time implicitly through relative position and attention sink structure, so eviction patterns interact destructively with RoPE or ALiBi embeddings in ways that aren't visible in perplexity on standard benchmarks. The expert worry is that learned scorers overfit to evaluation distributions where temporal coherence is testable, but silently degrade on long-horizon tasks (multi-step reasoning, longitudinal summarization) where the error only surfaces many thousands of tokens after the bad eviction decision.

The deeper issue is that no static proxy signal can be policy-agnostic: attention weight is an emergent property of which other tokens are present, so training a scorer offline under policy A and deploying under policy B is structurally similar to training a value function in one MDP and evaluating it in another with different transition dynamics.

Marginal importance — sometimes called "leave-one-out" (LOO) relevance, formalized in the context of transformers by work on attention attribution and influence functions (Koh & Liang 2017 for the general case; more recently in LLM pruning by Men et al., "ShortGPT," 2024) — looks cleaner because it's defined without reference to any specific cache policy: ablate token 
𝑡
t, measure output degradation, score accordingly. The problem is that LOO importance is additive-independence-blind: it measures each token's marginal contribution given all others are present, which systematically undervalues tokens that are redundant when the context is full but load-bearing when peers are evicted. For temporal reasoning specifically, this means temporal anchors — tokens like "before the merger" or "on the third day" — often score as low-marginal-importance because the model can reconstruct their content from surrounding context when nothing has been evicted; but once other tokens referencing that event are gone, the anchor becomes the sole carrier of that temporal fact, and its absence causes a cascade failure. This is structurally identical to the coalitional value problem in cooperative game theory: Shapley values distribute credit fairly across all removal orderings, while LOO only samples one ordering (the full-context one), and Lundberg & Lee (2017) showed the gap between LOO and Shapley can be arbitrarily large when features are correlated — which in language means syntactically or temporally co-referent tokens. Empirically, on multi-hop temporal benchmarks like TimeQA or the temporal subset of MuSiQue, models using LOO-scored eviction degrade faster than even simple recency baselines once chain length exceeds 3-4 hops, because the LOO scorer has systematically pruned the intermediate anchors that chain-of-thought reasoning would need to traverse.
